title: Query Plan Analysis: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Join Algorithms, Sorts, and Memory Spills
description: Query Plan Analysis: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Join Algorithms, Sorts, and Memory Spills. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Read plan nodes and compare estimates with actual execution.
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to localize work.
Compare nested-loop, hash, and merge joins by input shape.
Recognize sort/hash spills and temporary I/O.

mentalModel.text: A query plan is the database's step-by-step recipe for answering a query. Each step reads rows or combines results from steps below it. EXPLAIN shows the planned recipe and estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports what actually happened. Compare the estimate with reality and find where the work or surprise begins.

blocks.text: EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL expects to use. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and reports what actually happened.

EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL intends to use. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports measured row counts and timing. Be careful with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE: ANALYZE executes them, so use a safe test or transaction when appropriate.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42;

blocks.outcome: Read the plan as evidence: estimates describe the planner's expectations, while ANALYZE reports measured execution.

blocks.text: Cardinality is the number of rows a plan step is expected to produce. A large gap between estimated and actual rows can push the planner toward a poor join or sort strategy.

The planner guesses how many rows each step will produce. If it expects 900 rows but actually sees 120,000, later choices such as join order or sorting may be poor. Find the earliest step where the estimate is far off, then investigate stale statistics, uneven data, or filters that are related to each other.

blocks.problem: The plan estimates 900 active customers, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 120,000.
reasoning: Find the earliest node where estimated and actual row counts diverge.
Check whether statistics are stale or the data distribution is uneven; run ANALYZE when appropriate.
Re-check the plan before forcing a join type. First understand why the estimate was wrong.

blocks.text: Read the example plan from the bottom up. The sequential scan returns 120,000 rows even though the planner expected 900. The Sort must therefore order far more rows than expected, and its `external merge` plus temporary I/O shows that the sort spilled to disk. The first question is why the row estimate was wrong—not simply how to increase memory.

reasoning: Find the earliest node with a large estimated-versus-actual row gap; here it is the scan's filter.

Check whether statistics are stale and whether tenant sizes are highly uneven. Run `ANALYZE` if statistics need refreshing; consider extended statistics when correlated columns cause estimation errors.
Then re-read the plan. Correcting the estimate may change join order, access path, or sort strategy without forcing a plan node manually.
blocks.outcome: A downstream sort or join may be slow because an earlier row-count estimate was wrong. Diagnose the earliest divergence first.
blocks.problem: A plan estimates 900 rows from a tenant filter but actually returns 120,000.

blocks.text: A nested-loop join repeats an inner lookup for each outer row. A hash join builds a lookup structure for one side and probes it with the other.

A nested-loop join takes each row from one side and looks for matches on the other side, so it often works well when the outer side is small and the inner lookup is cheap. A hash join builds a lookup table for one side, and a merge join walks two ordered inputs. None is always best; input size and ordering matter.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT o.id,c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id;

blocks.problem: A nested-loop join performs 100,000 inner index lookups when the planner expected only 100 outer rows.
reasoning: Repeated inner work may dominate once the actual outer row count is much larger than expected.
A hash join may help for a large equality join, but it needs memory and may spill to disk.
Compare actual time, rows, loops, and buffers before deciding another join strategy is better.
blocks.outcome: Join algorithms are trade-offs. The right choice depends on row counts, indexes, memory, and data shape.

blocks.text: For a concrete comparison, joining 30 customers to their orders can suit a nested loop when each customer lookup uses an index and returns few rows. Joining hundreds of thousands of orders to customers may favor a hash or merge strategy. These are not fixed rules: inspect actual outer rows, inner `loops`, buffers, and whether inputs are already ordered.
A Sort node orders rows when no earlier step provides the requested order at an acceptable cost.

A Sort step arranges rows for ORDER BY or another operation that needs order. A matching index can sometimes provide that order, but using the index may still cost more than reading many rows and sorting them together.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100;

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.problem: A query filters orders by customer_id and sorts by created_at DESC before returning 20 rows.
reasoning: An index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) may provide the order directly.
Without a useful ordering index, PostgreSQL may sort all qualifying rows before applying LIMIT.
An index is not automatically better; compare the work needed to find rows with the work needed to sort them.
blocks.outcome: Look for Sort nodes and ask whether a suitable index can provide the requested order.

blocks.text: Sorts and hash joins use working memory. When a step needs more than it can keep in memory, PostgreSQL can use temporary disk space or process a hash join in batches.

Sorts and hash joins need working memory. If they need more than is available, PostgreSQL can write temporary data to disk or process a hash join in batches. Raising work_mem affects each operation and can multiply across many simultaneous queries, so don't increase it blindly. When a sort reports an “external merge,” it means PostgreSQL used temporary disk space rather than keeping the whole sort in memory.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT customer_id,sum(total_amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY sum(total_amount) DESC;

blocks.problem: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a sort using an external merge and large temporary reads/writes.
reasoning: The sort exceeded its available memory and used temporary files.
Check how many rows are sorted and whether an index can provide the order or earlier filters can reduce the input.
Increasing work_mem may help one query but is not a free global fix because many operations and sessions can use memory concurrently.
blocks.outcome: Reduce unnecessary work first, then tune memory with concurrency in mind.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A query slows after data growth. The planner estimates 900 rows, but execution produces 120,000 and the following sort spills to temporary disk. The first bad estimate may explain the later work.

2. Definition and design choice — EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan and estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and reports actual rows and timing. Read plan nodes from their inputs upward, comparing estimates with actuals to find where reality first diverges.

blocks.problem: A tenant filter is estimated to return 900 rows but actually returns 120,000. The next sort uses an external merge and writes about 24 MB of temporary data.
reasoning: Inspect the earliest row-estimate mismatch, then check statistics, skew, correlated predicates, and whether ANALYZE or extended statistics can improve the estimate.
The sort spill may be downstream of too many rows reaching the sort. Increasing work_mem may help but the setting can multiply across operations and concurrent sessions.
Planner cost units are not milliseconds, and parent-node time includes child work. Read actual rows, loops, buffers, and temporary I/O together.
blocks.outcome: Fix the underlying estimate or query shape, then compare plans on representative parameters. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on writes only in a safe test or transaction.

blocks.content: Planner costs are not milliseconds; parent timings include child work.

blocks.answer: ANALYZE executes the statement; use caution with writes.

questions.explanation: Large estimate errors can affect join strategy and expected memory use. Inspect predicates, statistics, and actual rows first; tune memory only with evidence and concurrency in mind.

interviewScenarios.prompt: An endpoint regresses after data growth. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a nested loop with a large outer input and hundreds of thousands of inner loops. Investigate.
strongAnswerPoints: Quantify repeated inner work with loops/buffers.
Check statistics, skew, join order, and alternate plans.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would find where estimates diverge, quantify inner work and buffers, then check statistics, skew, and whether the inner lookup is selective. Test targeted changes against the same workload and verify result correctness.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A report's Sort node shows disk usage and temp I/O. What do you do before raising work_mem globally?
strongAnswerPoints: Check sort input size and whether ordering is necessary.
See if an index or earlier filtering reduces work.
Estimate memory multiplied across operations and concurrent sessions.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Inspect input rows and plan shape first. If memory is the bottleneck, estimate concurrency and test a scoped setting. A global increase can multiply memory use across sessions.
